chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Mom Charleston and Mom Havelow in Philadelphia
summary: Jackson recalls the big cook Mom Charleston and Mom Havelow's brownstone where bandleaders lived upstairs.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: And there was Mom Charleston in Philadelphia.
Moms --
Charleston.
In Philadelphia?
Yeah, she was a big fat --
Havelow.
No, Mom Havelow too, but Mom Charleston was before her.
Oh, is that so?
Oh, yeah. Now, Mom Charleston used to be up the street around the corner from the Lincoln Theater --
I see.
-- when the Lincoln was at Broad and Lombard, you see.
I see.
And she was a big woman and she could
cook. She could cook like everything. We used to go over there and just -- Don Redman -- we used to go -- Don Redman was a eater too, you know.
He was a fantastic eater. And we used to go in Mom Charleston's and eat.
Mom [Havelow] was great, too.
She had a whole brownstone house and --
That's right.
-- you ate in the basement, right?
That's right.
On the first floor the bandleaders lived. There was an apartment there with a piano in it where Basie or Duke, whatever the bandleader, was in. Remember that?
Sure.
We don't know how many tunes -- God knows how many tunes that Duke wrote on that old piano in Mom [Havelow's] first floor.
Oh, yes.
All of the sidemen had to go way up-stairs to stay.
That's right, that's right.
